title: Bronchiectasis: Confirm the Pattern, Treat Exacerbations, Protect Lung Function
bottomLine: Bronchiectasis is persistent abnormal airway dilatation with chronic infection/inflammation. Confirm it with the appropriate chest imaging, identify a treatable cause, obtain sputum microbiology when clinically useful, and manage exacerbations, airway clearance and recurrent-infection risk rather than treating every chronic cough as repeated uncomplicated bronchitis.
recognize: Chronic productive cough, recurrent lower-respiratory infections, daily sputum, hemoptysis and persistent crackles raise suspicion.
Frequent exacerbations, prior severe infection, immune deficiency, aspiration, inflammatory disease or cystic fibrosis can be underlying clues.
differentiate: COPD and asthma can coexist, but recurrent purulent sputum and repeated focal infections should trigger a bronchiectasis differential.
An acute increase in cough, sputum quantity/purulence, dyspnea or systemic symptoms can represent an exacerbation; baseline colonization alone is not proof that every symptom requires antibiotics.
assessment: Assess exacerbation frequency, sputum volume/colour, hemoptysis, dyspnea, oxygenation, weight/nutrition, aspiration risk, smoking/exposures and prior organisms/resistance.
Review vaccination, airway-clearance technique and medications that may worsen secretion retention.
workup: High-resolution CT is central to structural confirmation; obtain spirometry and cause-directed testing.

Send sputum culture during clinically important exacerbations or when persistent infection/resistance will change treatment; evaluate for nontuberculous mycobacteria or other pathogens when the pattern warrants specialist workup.
management: Use individualized airway-clearance therapy and pulmonary rehabilitation/exercise where appropriate.
Treat bacterial exacerbations with organism/history-appropriate antibiotics and reassess failure rather than repeatedly broadening empiric therapy.
Refer frequent exacerbations, recurrent hemoptysis, declining lung function or complex infection to respirology/bronchiectasis care.
medicationSafety: Long-term macrolide or inhaled-antibiotic strategies require specialist selection, interaction/QT review and microbiologic context; they are not routine for every patient.
Bronchodilators/inhaled corticosteroids are used for relevant coexisting airflow disease, not automatically because bronchiectasis is present.
redFlags: Recurrent infection with resistant or unusual organisms
counselling: Teach airway-clearance adherence, vaccination, early exacerbation recognition, hydration and when hemoptysis requires urgent care.
followUp: Track exacerbation burden, microbiology, symptoms and lung function; review whether recurrent antibiotic use is treating a true exacerbation pattern.
examTrap: Treating chronic colonization or stable daily sputum as a new bacterial exacerbation without a clinical change.
oneLinePearl: Bronchiectasis care is airway clearance plus cause/infection control—not endless empiric antibiotics.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society respiratory practice and bronchiectasis assembly resources
Canadian antimicrobial stewardship principles

title: Pulmonary Hypertension: Recognize Right-Heart Strain and Refer by Cause
bottomLine: Pulmonary hypertension is a hemodynamic syndrome with multiple causes, not a diagnosis made from one echocardiographic pressure estimate. Recognize unexplained exertional dyspnea, syncope and right-heart failure, investigate common cardiac/lung/thromboembolic causes, and refer suspected pulmonary arterial or chronic thromboembolic disease for definitive specialist classification.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pressure, presyncope/syncope, edema, elevated JVP and a loud P2 can occur.
Advanced disease may present with hypoxemia, RV failure or low-output symptoms.
differentiate: Left-heart disease, chronic lung disease/hypoxia and chronic thromboembolic disease are common causes and require different management from pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Echocardiography estimates probability and RV effects; right-heart catheterization is required for definitive hemodynamic classification when advanced therapy is considered.
assessment: Assess exertional limitation, syncope, edema, oxygenation, connective-tissue disease, prior VTE, liver disease, HIV/drug exposure, sleep-disordered breathing and pregnancy status.
Examine for RV failure and alternative cardiopulmonary causes.
workup: Use ECG, chest imaging, echocardiography, pulmonary function testing and cause-directed labs; evaluate chronic thromboembolic disease with the appropriate pulmonary vascular pathway.
Do not rely on estimated pulmonary artery pressure alone without assessing RV structure/function and the clinical cause.
management: Treat the underlying cause and associated hypoxemia/volume overload while arranging specialist assessment.
Pulmonary arterial hypertension therapies are diagnosis/class-specific and should not be started empirically for undifferentiated PH.
Pregnancy with significant pulmonary arterial hypertension is very high risk and needs urgent multidisciplinary specialty care.
medicationSafety: Aggressive diuresis can worsen preload-dependent low output; titrate volume management to congestion and perfusion.
Some PAH drugs have major pregnancy, hypotension, hepatic or interaction considerations and require specialist oversight.
counselling: Explain that pulmonary hypertension has different groups/causes and treatment depends on confirming which mechanism is present.
followUp: Close the loop on echocardiography, thromboembolic evaluation and specialist referral; worsening syncope or edema warrants earlier reassessment.
examTrap: Starting pulmonary-arterial-hypertension therapy from an elevated echo-estimated pressure before determining whether the patient has left-heart, lung or thromboembolic disease.
oneLinePearl: PH is a syndrome; classify the cause before choosing the drug.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Thoracic Society Position Statement on Pulmonary Hypertension — current
Canadian pulmonary vascular practice

title: Sarcoidosis: Confirm Compatible Granulomatous Disease and Screen Organ Risk
bottomLine: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous diagnosis of compatibility plus exclusion. Not every bilateral hilar-adenopathy pattern requires immediate steroids; first establish the clinical syndrome, exclude important infectious/malignant mimics, identify organ-threatening disease, and treat only when symptoms or organ risk justify therapy.
recognize: Pulmonary symptoms, bilateral hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, uveitis, erythema nodosum, hypercalcemia, conduction disease and neurologic involvement are possible.
Many patients are asymptomatic or have self-limited disease.
differentiate: Tuberculosis, fungal infection, lymphoma, occupational exposure and drug reactions can mimic granulomatous disease.
Elevated ACE is neither sufficiently sensitive nor specific to diagnose sarcoidosis by itself.
assessment: Assess respiratory symptoms, visual symptoms, palpitations/syncope, neurologic deficits, skin/joint findings, calcium symptoms, exposures and infection risk.
workup: Use chest imaging and pulmonary function testing; obtain tissue confirmation when diagnosis is uncertain or treatment/risk demands it, selecting the safest high-yield site.
Screen for clinically important ocular, cardiac, calcium/renal and other organ involvement according to presentation and specialty guidance.
management: Observe stable low-risk disease when appropriate.
Use corticosteroids or steroid-sparing therapy for significant symptomatic or organ-threatening disease with specialist input.
Cardiac, neurologic or severe ocular involvement warrants urgent specialty assessment.
medicationSafety: Before prolonged immunosuppression, assess infection risk, vaccination and steroid complications; monitor therapy-specific toxicity.
Do not suppress granulomatous inflammation before reasonably excluding infection when the presentation makes TB/fungal disease plausible.
counselling: Explain that sarcoidosis may affect organs outside the lung and that treatment depends on risk, not the X-ray appearance alone.
followUp: Track symptoms, lung function and organ-specific risk; reassess an atypical course for an alternate diagnosis.
examTrap: Diagnosing sarcoidosis from hilar adenopathy plus elevated ACE and immediately starting steroids without considering infection or lymphoma.
oneLinePearl: Sarcoidosis is compatible granulomatous disease after important mimics are excluded.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society interstitial/granulomatous respiratory practice resources
Canadian specialty practice principles

title: Adult Cystic Fibrosis: Complex Multisystem Care Belongs With a CF Centre
bottomLine: Adults with cystic fibrosis require coordinated specialist CF-centre care even when highly effective modulator therapy has improved symptoms. The NP must recognize pulmonary exacerbation, CF-related diabetes, nutrition, liver/bone disease, fertility/pregnancy and medication-interaction issues, while avoiding generic non-CF antibiotic or infection-control assumptions.
recognize: Increasing cough/sputum, dyspnea, fatigue, reduced lung function, weight loss or hemoptysis can signal a pulmonary exacerbation.
Adults may also have CF-related diabetes, pancreatic insufficiency, liver disease, sinus disease, bone disease and fertility/reproductive issues.
differentiate: CF pulmonary exacerbations are individualized and often informed by prior respiratory cultures; standard community pneumonia algorithms may not cover chronic CF organisms.
CF-related diabetes has distinct screening/treatment considerations and should not simply be managed as ordinary type 2 diabetes.
assessment: Assess respiratory trajectory, prior microbiology, modulator/airway-clearance adherence, nutrition/weight, glucose symptoms, GI/liver issues, pregnancy plans and medication access/interactions.
workup: Coordinate spirometry, respiratory cultures and CF-centre testing; investigate complications through current Canadian CF standards.
Do not assume improved symptoms on a CFTR modulator remove the need for routine specialist surveillance.
management: Coordinate exacerbation therapy with the CF centre whenever possible, using previous susceptibility and individual history.
Continue airway-clearance/nutrition/pancreatic and complication management according to the current CF plan.
CFTR modulators require genotype/indication, interaction and monitoring review through current Canadian guidance.
medicationSafety: CFTR modulators have important drug interactions and monitoring requirements; verify the current Canadian product/CF-centre plan.
Avoid cross-infection between people with CF in healthcare settings and follow CF-specific infection-prevention practices.
counselling: Reinforce that modulator success does not mean CF surveillance is finished and encourage early CF-team contact for pulmonary change.
followUp: Maintain CF-centre follow-up and closed-loop management of cultures, lung function, nutrition, CFRD and other multisystem complications.
examTrap: Treating an adult with CF pulmonary deterioration as routine CAP without reviewing prior CF microbiology or contacting the CF team.
oneLinePearl: CF care is individualized, culture-informed and centre-coordinated—even in the modulator era.
sourceBasis: Cystic Fibrosis Canada — Canadian Guidelines for Cystic Fibrosis Care
Cystic Fibrosis Canada pulmonary-exacerbation and CFTR-modulator guidelines

title: Mechanical Ventilation for the NP: Oxygenation, Ventilation, Pressures, and Harm
bottomLine: Ventilator numbers are physiology, not settings to change in isolation. Separate oxygenation failure from ventilation failure, assess the patient and waveform/pressure pattern, use lung-protective principles when appropriate, and recognize sudden deterioration as a potential tube, circuit, pneumothorax, secretion or hemodynamic emergency.
recognize: FiO2/PEEP primarily influence oxygenation; minute ventilation and effective alveolar ventilation drive CO2 clearance.
High peak pressure with unchanged plateau suggests increased airway resistance; elevated peak and plateau pressures suggest reduced compliance or excessive delivered volume/pressure.
differentiate: Hypoxemia from derecruitment/ARDS differs from hypercapnia due to inadequate ventilation or airflow obstruction.
A ventilated patient who acutely deteriorates requires immediate bedside evaluation before assuming the ventilator merely needs a higher setting.
assessment: Assess airway/tube position, chest movement, breath sounds, SpO2, hemodynamics, sedation/synchrony, secretions and recent changes.
Review ABG/VBG context, delivered tidal volume, respiratory rate, PEEP, FiO2 and relevant airway/plateau pressures.
workup: Use blood gas and chest imaging when they answer the problem; evaluate suspected pneumothorax, mucus plugging, tube migration or pulmonary edema promptly.
Interpret ventilator alarms by the clinical problem rather than silencing or repeatedly resetting them.
management: If life-threatening deterioration occurs, call for immediate critical-care/airway support and ensure effective oxygenation/ventilation; manual ventilation may be required while the cause is assessed.
Use lung-protective ventilation for ARDS/at-risk lungs and avoid unnecessary high FiO2 or injurious pressures.
Treat the underlying cause and reassess gas exchange/hemodynamics after changes.
medicationSafety: Sedation and neuromuscular blockade can worsen hypotension, delirium and prolonged ventilation and require indication-specific monitoring.
PEEP/positive pressure can reduce venous return and worsen hypotension, especially in preload-sensitive states.
counselling: For families, explain the goals of ventilation and that settings are adjusted to physiology and lung protection rather than to make every blood gas immediately normal.
followUp: Trend gas exchange, pressures, hemodynamics and readiness to reduce support; coordinate weaning/extubation assessment with critical care/RT.
examTrap: Responding to sudden ventilated-patient hypoxemia by increasing FiO2 and walking away without checking tube position, pneumothorax, obstruction or circuit failure.
oneLinePearl: Ventilator deterioration is a bedside emergency before it is a settings problem.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society home/respiratory ventilation guideline library
Canadian critical-care lung-protective ventilation principles

title: Asthma–COPD Overlap: Preserve Asthma Safety While Treating Persistent Obstruction
bottomLine: Patients can have persistent COPD-like obstruction plus convincing asthma biology/history. Do not treat the label as a third disease with one fixed regimen: confirm airflow obstruction, identify asthma features and exacerbation risk, preserve inhaled-corticosteroid-containing therapy when asthma is present, and add long-acting bronchodilation according to symptoms and COPD physiology.
recognize: Asthma clues include variable symptoms, earlier-life disease, atopy and meaningful reversibility/variability; COPD clues include persistent post-bronchodilator obstruction plus smoking or inhalational exposure history.
Frequent exacerbations, eosinophilic inflammation and inhaler technique/adherence affect treatment decisions.
differentiate: Do not diagnose overlap solely because one bronchodilator test shows partial reversibility; COPD can be reversible and asthma can become fixed.
Heart failure, bronchiectasis and other causes of chronic dyspnea/wheeze may mimic both.
assessment: Review symptom variability, exacerbations, smoking/exposures, eosinophil context, atopy, pneumonia history, inhaler technique and adherence.
workup: Confirm persistent obstruction with spirometry and use asthma/COPD-specific diagnostic criteria rather than symptom labels alone.
Evaluate alternative diagnoses when severity or progression is atypical.
management: When asthma is convincingly present, include ICS-containing controller therapy and avoid LABA monotherapy.
Add/optimize long-acting bronchodilation according to COPD symptom/exacerbation burden and individualized risk.
Provide smoking cessation, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation/activity and action-plan education.
medicationSafety: ICS increases pneumonia/oral-candidiasis risks in some COPD-predominant patients, but withdrawing ICS indiscriminately from true asthma can be dangerous.
Review duplicate inhaler classes and device complexity.
counselling: Teach why one inhaler may protect against asthma risk while another improves fixed obstruction; demonstrate device technique.
followUp: Track symptoms, exacerbations, spirometry when indicated, eosinophil/risk context and adverse effects.
examTrap: Using LABA alone in a patient with convincing asthma features because the spirometry also looks like COPD.
oneLinePearl: If asthma is truly in the mix, preserve asthma-safe ICS-containing therapy while treating COPD physiology.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society asthma and COPD guideline library — current
CTS asthma/COPD knowledge tools

title: Respiratory Infection in Immunocompromise: Broaden the Differential, Not Just the Antibiotic
bottomLine: An immunocompromised patient with respiratory symptoms may deteriorate with minimal fever or leukocytosis and may have bacterial, viral, fungal, Pneumocystis, mycobacterial or noninfectious pulmonary disease. Determine immune defect, severity, timing and imaging pattern, obtain high-yield microbiology, and escalate early instead of simply prescribing broader outpatient antibiotics.
recognize: Hypoxemia, tachypnea, subtle confusion, declining exercise tolerance or diffuse infiltrates may precede dramatic systemic signs.
The likely pathogens differ after transplant, chemotherapy/neutropenia, prolonged corticosteroids, biologic therapy, advanced HIV or congenital immune disease.
differentiate: Drug pneumonitis, pulmonary edema, malignancy, alveolar hemorrhage and inflammatory lung disease can mimic infection.
A normal chest radiograph early in Pneumocystis or other infection does not always end the workup when hypoxemia and risk are high.
assessment: Define the immune defect, recent neutrophil count, transplant timing, immunosuppressants/steroids, prophylaxis, exposures, travel, oxygenation and tempo.
Assess whether the patient can safely remain outpatient.
workup: Use chest imaging and targeted cultures/PCR/antigen testing; pursue bronchoscopy or specialty diagnostics when noninvasive testing is insufficient and the patient is high risk.
Obtain cultures before therapy when feasible without delaying life-saving treatment.
management: Unstable, hypoxemic, neutropenic or rapidly progressive disease needs hospital/specialty management.
Choose empiric treatment based on immune defect, syndrome, local microbiology and prophylaxis history—not simply the broadest community regimen.
Consider noninfectious etiologies when response is poor.
medicationSafety: Renal/hepatic function and drug interactions matter because antifungals, antivirals and transplant drugs can interact substantially.
Do not stop prophylaxis or immunosuppression reflexively without specialty input unless an acute toxicity/emergency requires action.
counselling: Teach lower thresholds for urgent reassessment because classic fever/inflammation may be muted.
followUp: Close the loop on cultures/PCR and ensure antimicrobial de-escalation or alternative-diagnosis reassessment when results return.
examTrap: Reassuring a heavily immunosuppressed patient because they are afebrile and the WBC count is not elevated.
oneLinePearl: In immunocompromise, absence of inflammation is not absence of danger.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society ILD/immunosuppression infection-screening resources
Canadian infectious disease stewardship principles

title: Thoracentesis: Know Why You Are Sampling or Draining the Pleural Space
bottomLine: Thoracentesis is diagnostic, therapeutic, or both. Confirm a pleural effusion, decide what question the fluid must answer, use image guidance and procedural safety standards, and recognize pneumothorax, bleeding, infection and re-expansion complications promptly.
recognize: New or unexplained unilateral/asymmetric effusion, suspected infection or malignancy, and symptomatic large effusions are common reasons for pleural sampling/drainage.
Small stable bilateral effusions in a clear heart-failure context may not need immediate diagnostic thoracentesis if they respond as expected.
differentiate: Transudative and exudative mechanisms guide the differential; classification requires paired pleural/serum context rather than visual appearance alone.
An empyema/complicated parapneumonic effusion may require chest drainage rather than repeated simple aspiration.
assessment: Assess respiratory status, effusion size/location, anticoagulants/bleeding risk, platelets/coagulation context, ability to cooperate and procedural anatomy.
workup: Use ultrasound to locate fluid and improve procedural safety; send pleural studies matched to the clinical question, commonly protein/LDH, cell count/differential, pH/glucose, microbiology and cytology when indicated.
Do not order every pleural test indiscriminately.
management: Perform or refer according to NP scope/local privileging and image-guided procedure standards.
Stop and assess if the patient develops significant chest pain, respiratory distress, hypotension or other complication.
Drainage strategy for large/chronic effusions is individualized to symptoms and risk.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulation/antiplatelet management is patient-, drug- and procedure-specific; follow current local procedural policy instead of memorizing one universal hold interval.
Avoid unnecessary correction of mildly abnormal coagulation tests when current procedure guidance does not support it.
counselling: Explain the diagnostic question, expected sensations and warning symptoms after the procedure.
followUp: Review fluid results and ensure the result changes the etiologic plan; reassess recurrence and need for pleural specialty care.
examTrap: Performing diagnostic thoracentesis on every small bilateral heart-failure effusion without asking whether the result will change management.
oneLinePearl: Before the needle, know the pleural question you are trying to answer.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society chest-procedure practice resources
Choosing Wisely Canada procedure stewardship principles

title: Occupational Lung Disease: The Exposure History Is a Diagnostic Test
bottomLine: Work-related asthma, pneumoconiosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis and toxic inhalational disease are often missed because occupation is recorded as a job title instead of an exposure history. Ask what the patient actually breathes, timing relative to work, co-worker illness and protective controls, then connect physiologic/imaging findings to exposure and occupational-health action.
recognize: Symptoms improving away from work suggest occupational asthma but are not required.
Dusts, silica/asbestos, metal fumes, isocyanates, animal/organic antigens and acute irritants produce different syndromes.
differentiate: Work-exacerbated pre-existing asthma differs from new sensitizer-induced occupational asthma but both require exposure control.
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis and pneumoconiosis are not treated as ordinary COPD simply because dyspnea is chronic.
assessment: Obtain current and past jobs, specific agents/tasks, ventilation/PPE, temporal relation of symptoms, accidental high-dose exposures, smoking, hobbies and co-worker patterns.
Ask about compensation/reporting implications without allowing administrative concerns to delay care.
workup: Use spirometry/bronchodilator testing, serial peak-flow or challenge strategy, diffusion testing and imaging according to suspected disease.
Specialist/occupational medicine evaluation may be required to establish work relatedness.
management: Reduce/remove harmful exposure when clinically indicated and coordinate workplace controls/occupational health.
Treat the actual respiratory disease while documenting objective exposure-disease evidence.
Urgent toxic inhalation or rapidly progressive disease belongs on an acute-care pathway.
medicationSafety: Medication cannot substitute for continued uncontrolled exposure; escalating inhalers while leaving a sensitizer exposure unchanged may allow disease progression.
redFlags: Suspected significant silica/asbestos exposure with concerning imaging
counselling: Encourage specific exposure documentation and safe workplace controls; explain that work-related disease can occur despite smoking or other competing risks.
followUp: Track symptoms/lung function relative to exposure changes and close referrals/reporting requirements according to jurisdiction.
examTrap: Writing 'construction worker' in social history without asking about silica, asbestos, welding fumes, masks, ventilation or symptom timing.
oneLinePearl: Occupation is not the exposure—the task and inhalant are.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society occupational/environmental lung health resources
Canadian occupational medicine practice principles

title: Pulmonary Function Testing: Identify the Physiologic Pattern Before Naming the Disease
bottomLine: PFT interpretation starts with test quality and physiology: obstruction, restriction, gas-transfer abnormality and bronchodilator response. Spirometry can suggest restriction but cannot confirm total-lung-capacity reduction; a bronchodilator response supports variable airflow physiology but does not by itself define asthma or exclude COPD.
recognize: Obstruction is identified from the FEV1/FVC relationship using appropriate reference/lower-limit criteria rather than a one-size fixed ratio in every patient.
Restriction requires reduced total lung capacity; low FVC on spirometry alone may reflect restriction, air trapping, poor effort or mixed disease.
DLCO helps contextualize emphysema, ILD, pulmonary vascular disease, anemia and other gas-transfer problems.
differentiate: A normal spirometry result does not exclude intermittent asthma when the patient is asymptomatic at testing.
Low FVC plus obstruction may represent air trapping rather than true restriction; obtain lung volumes when it matters.
assessment: Confirm indication, smoking/exposure history, inhaler timing, symptoms, effort/technique and whether reference values fit the patient.
workup: Interpret quality first, then FEV1/FVC, FEV1/FVC pattern, lung volumes when available, DLCO and bronchodilator response.
Use bronchoprovocation or other testing selectively when asthma remains suspected despite nondiagnostic spirometry.
management: Use the physiologic pattern to refine the differential and next test; do not prescribe solely from a PFT label without clinical correlation.
Refer unexplained restriction, severe diffusion impairment, mixed defects or discordant symptoms for specialist assessment.
medicationSafety: Withholding bronchodilator before testing should follow the lab protocol and clinical safety; do not provoke severe symptoms merely to obtain a cleaner test.
Review inhaler technique/adherence before declaring treatment failure from persistent obstruction.
redFlags: Symptoms far out of proportion to spirometry
counselling: Explain that PFTs describe lung physiology and must be combined with symptoms, exposures and imaging to establish a diagnosis.
followUp: Repeat testing when clinically indicated to assess trajectory or treatment response, not on an automatic schedule without a question.
examTrap: Diagnosing restriction because FVC is low on spirometry without confirming total lung capacity.
oneLinePearl: PFTs name the physiologic defect first; the clinician names the disease second.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society pulmonary-function standards and guideline resources
CTS asthma/COPD diagnostic guidance
